explanations.answer: Leave and live as foreigners wherever they can
explanations.explanation: That's exactly it, baker. Elisha tells her, "Arise, you and your household; go and live as a foreigner wherever you can." The reason he gives is that the LORD has decreed a seven-year famine for the land (2 Kings 8:1). So she doesn't dig in. She packs up and goes.

explanations.answer: Stay home and store up all the grain they can
explanations.explanation: Stocking up sounds smart, friend. I'd have bought a whole pallet of flour myself. But Elisha doesn't say stay. He tells her to go and live as a foreigner wherever she can (2 Kings 8:1). That's a whole different plan than a full pantry.

explanations.answer: Move inside the walls of Samaria and wait it out
explanations.explanation: Walls feel safe, I get it. But Elisha never mentions Samaria or any walls here. He says, "Arise, you and your household; go and live as a foreigner wherever you can." That means leaving the land, not tucking in tighter (2 Kings 8:1).

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The text says she and her household lived as foreigners for seven years in the land of the Philistines (2 Kings 8:2). Seven years is a long time to be the new neighbor. I once waited that long in a drawer, and at least she had a view.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. The text says she and her household lived as foreigners for seven years in the land of the Philistines (2 Kings 8:2). So the seven years and the Philistines both hold up. Nothing in that verse is mixed up.

explanations.answer: king
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. She went to the king to appeal for her house and her land (2 Kings 8:3). Seven years away, and she heads straight to the top. I think that takes some nerve.

explanations.answer: elders
explanations.explanation: Elders are a fair guess, friend. But the text says she went to the king to appeal for her house and her land (2 Kings 8:3). No elders show up in this passage at all.

explanations.answer: priest
explanations.explanation: I see why a priest comes to mind. But the verse is plain: she went to the king to appeal for her house and her land (2 Kings 8:3). No priest anywhere in this scene.

explanations.answer: All the great things Elisha has done
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker! The king says to Gehazi, "Please relate to me all the great things Elisha has done." Gehazi is the servant of the man of God, so he has stories (2 Kings 8:4). I'd pay good money to hear that whole list.

explanations.answer: Where Elisha has been staying lately
explanations.explanation: Good guess if the king wanted a visit, friend. But the text never says that. The king asks Gehazi to relate all the great things Elisha has done (2 Kings 8:4). He wants the stories, not an address.

explanations.answer: Why the famine lasted so many years
explanations.explanation: The famine is a big part of this passage, so I get it. But the king's request is different. He says, "Please relate to me all the great things Elisha has done" (2 Kings 8:4). Nothing about why the famine lasted.

explanations.answer: The woman whose son Elisha revived
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! Gehazi is telling about the dead brought back to life, and just then the woman whose son Elisha had revived comes to appeal for her house and her land (2 Kings 8:5). That timing is something else. I can't even get my timer to cooperate with me.

explanations.answer: Elisha the man of God himself
explanations.explanation: Elisha is the star of the story being told, so I see the pull. But he isn't the one who walks in. The one who comes in is the woman whose son Elisha had revived (2 Kings 8:5).

explanations.answer: A messenger from Ben-hadad of Aram
explanations.explanation: Ben-hadad was king of Aram, and he does show up elsewhere in these chapters. But not here. Just then, the woman whose son Elisha had revived comes in to appeal to the king (2 Kings 8:5).

explanations.answer: This is the woman and her son Elisha revived
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! Gehazi says, "My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is the son Elisha restored to life." He points right at the very people in his story (2 Kings 8:5). Talk about a live example.

explanations.answer: This woman should come back another day
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. Gehazi doesn't send her away at all. He says, "My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is the son Elisha restored to life" (2 Kings 8:5). He introduces her on the spot.

explanations.answer: This woman must speak with Elisha first
explanations.explanation: Close to something a careful servant might say, but not what's written. Gehazi says, "My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is the son Elisha restored to life" (2 Kings 8:5). He doesn't send her to Elisha. He presents her to the king himself.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. She doesn't say Gehazi has it mixed up. When the king asked her, she confirmed it (2 Kings 8:6). So Gehazi's story held up.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. When the king asked the woman, she confirmed it (2 Kings 8:6). She says Gehazi has it right, not mixed up. I think that's the best kind of agreement to walk into.

explanations.answer: field
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The king says, "Restore all that was hers, along with all the proceeds of the field from the day that she left the country until now" (2 Kings 8:6). Her house and land come back, plus what the field produced. That's a whole lot more than she asked for.

explanations.answer: flocks
explanations.explanation: Flocks make sense on a farm, friend. But the king's order mentions "all the proceeds of the field" (2 Kings 8:6). Flocks aren't in the verse.

explanations.answer: servants
explanations.explanation: I can see why servants came to mind. But the king's words are "all the proceeds of the field" (2 Kings 8:6). Servants aren't mentioned in his order.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Not this one, baker. The king says, "Restore all that was hers, along with all the proceeds of the field from the day that she left the country until now" (2 Kings 8:6). That starts from the day she left, not the day she came back. Seven years of field proceeds are in that order.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right, baker! The order covers the proceeds of the field "from the day that she left the country until now" (2 Kings 8:6). So it reaches back to the day she left. That's a long stretch, and the king didn't skip a year.
